analysis.one_liner: Strips states' power to require chemical and radiation warnings on everyday products.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee and died when the Congress ended, so no state or federal warning-label rules were changed.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Fair Packaging and Labeling Act so that no state, city, or federal agency could require a warning, ingredient list, or other notice about chemicals or radiation in a consumer product unless it met strict new federal standards [S2] [S3]. It would exempt trace amounts (below 0.1 percent), naturally occurring substances, trade secrets, and anything below a defined "de minimis" cancer-risk level, and it would let companies satisfy warnings with an on-package QR code and phone number instead of a printed label [S3]. A company that disliked a state rule could sue that state in federal court the day the rule was enacted, before any compliance deadline, and the state would bear the burden of proving its rule met the new standards [S3]. The practical target was state right-to-know warning laws, most famously California's Proposition 65 cancer warnings, which manufacturers have long sought to preempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers, retailers, and suppliers of consumer products, food, and chemicals gain if the bill passes: they would face far fewer state warning requirements, could replace on-package warnings with a digital link, could withhold trade-secret chemical identities, and would gain a new federal lawsuit tool to strike down state rules they disliked. State health agencies and consumers lose access to warning labels they currently rely on.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any state, locality, or federal agency from maintaining a chemical or radiation warning requirement unless it satisfies seven federal standards, including exemptions for constituents below 0.1 percent, naturally occurring substances, and trade secrets.
Allows companies to meet warning requirements with a QR code labeled "Scan here for more" and a phone number rather than information printed on the package.

Lets a manufacturer, retailer, or supplier sue a state in federal court starting the day the state enacts a labeling law — before compliance or enforcement begins — and puts the burden on the state to prove its rule complies, or the company is freed from it.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers pay with less information: warnings about cancer-causing or toxic chemicals in products they buy could disappear, shrink to a QR code many shoppers won't scan, or be hidden behind a trade-secret exemption. State health and consumer-protection agencies lose a tool they use to warn the public, and they would bear the legal burden of defending their own rules in court.

drawbacks.text: The trade-secret exemption would let companies withhold the identity of a chemical in a product, so a consumer could be told a product contains a listed substance without being told which one.

Electronic labeling would replace on-package warnings with a scannable link and phone call option, which works poorly for shoppers without smartphones and for products sold without packaging access at the point of decision.

The bill does not limit its preemption to truly baseless warnings: any state rule that fails the new 'risk-based' and 'best available science' standards — including rules built on hazard-based lists like California's — could be struck down in court, even for substances still present in meaningful amounts up to 0.1 percent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal — labels that are clear, accurate, and scientifically grounded — is legitimate, and some Prop 65-style warnings are arguably overbroad. But the bill's method is blanket preemption: it sweeps up every state and local warning law, hands companies a day-one lawsuit to challenge them, shifts the burden of proof to the state, and carves out trade secrets. The cost to consumers of losing accessible on-package warnings, particularly the QR-code substitution and trade-secret carve-out, outweighs the modest gain in label tidiness.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Kinzinger introduced the bill on June 6, 2018, with 13 cosponsors split 7 Democrats and 6 Republicans, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The committee took no further action; the complete action history shows only introduction and referral, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, killing the bill and wiping its slate clean.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, states kept their authority to require chemical and radiation warnings on products, and consumers kept the existing warning labels those laws provide. Manufacturers that wanted preemption gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States and consumers kept warning labels

for.name: Rep. Adam Kinzinger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 13 cosponsors.

for.name: Coalition for Accurate Product Labels
for.role: Industry coalition of chemical, food, and consumer product manufacturers and retailers
for.what_they_did: Backed the Accurate Labels Act and its predecessors, which were drafted to preempt state warning-label suits.

against.name: Rep. Greg Walden
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or committee vote; it sat without action after referral.

against.name: Consumer, health, and environmental advocacy groups
against.role: Public-interest organizations such as Environmental Working Group and NRDC
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as a gutting of state right-to-know warning laws like California's Proposition 65.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and the cosponsors split evenly, 7 Democrats and 6 Republicans, so the fight did not follow party lines; the bill died quietly in committee rather than in a partisan vote.

industries.note: The bill would preempt state warnings about chemicals in consumer products, including substances up to 0.1 percent concentration and trade-secret ingredients, and give manufacturers a federal suit to strike down state rules. Consumers would learn less about carcinogens and toxins in products they buy.

industries.industry: Consumer product, food, and retail companies
industries.note: Retailers and branded-product makers face frequent warning-label litigation under state laws like California's Proposition 65. The bill would let them replace printed warnings with a QR code and phone number and would let them sue states the day a labeling law is enacted.

industries.industry: State and local public-health and consumer-protection agencies
industries.note: These agencies issue and enforce warning requirements; the bill would forbid any requirement that fails the new federal standards and force them to defend their own rules in court at their own expense.
